geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (the island figure is BLS's own and is not summed from the 78; the observatory's derived island values are calculated from BLS's island figures)
name: How jobs, work sites and wages are counted (Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages)
plain: Jobs, work sites, wages and industries come from a US government count of jobs at employers who pay into the unemployment insurance system, which covers most wage-and-salary work. It counts jobs where the work is done, gives one annual average per year, and hides cells that would identify one employer.
definition: The Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) is built by the US Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) from the reports that employers file for unemployment insurance. The observatory reads its annual-average files for each of the 78 municipalities and for Puerto Rico. Employment is the average of twelve monthly counts; a monthly count is the number of covered workers who worked or were paid in the pay period that includes the 12th of the month. Establishments are the average of four quarterly counts of work sites. Wages are the total paid in the year. Every figure belongs to the place of the employer's work site, not to the place where the worker lives. Each figure is split by ownership (private or government) and by industry, using the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS).

coverage.frequency: One annual-average file per area and year. When the observatory's data are rebuilt, it checks whether BLS has published a newer year. It downloads each file once and reads it again only on a full refresh. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the files were downloaded on 3 October 2026, and 2025 is the latest year and is preliminary.

method: (1) The observatory finds the latest year by asking BLS for the San Juan file of the next year, starting from 2024, and reads every year from 2014 to that latest year. (2) For each year it downloads one file per area: 78 municipality codes and the island code 72000. (3) From each file it keeps the all-industry rows (industry code 10) for ownership codes 0, 1, 2, 3 and 5, and, for ownership 5 only, the 19 two-digit NAICS sectors and the three-digit codes 721 and 722. (4) It reads four columns: annual_avg_estabs, annual_avg_emplvl, total_annual_wages and avg_annual_pay. If the row's disclosure_code is N, all four are left blank. (5) Publication: ownership 0 gives qcew_estabs, qcew_jobs, qcew_wages and qcew_avg_pay. Ownership 5 gives qcew_private_jobs, the 19 industry variables, accommodation_jobs (721) and food_service_jobs (722). qcew_gov_jobs is qcew_jobs minus qcew_private_jobs, and gov_job_share_pct is that difference divided by qcew_jobs times 100. tourism_jobs is sector 72 plus sector 71 (sector 72 alone where 71 is blank). industry_hhi is the Herfindahl index of the published sectors and government. The data file also holds extras.top_sector, the largest employer group of each place and year (see its entry). jobs_per_employed_resident divides qcew_jobs by the American Community Survey count of employed residents of the same year label. BLS values are published as read. The observatory rounds its own calculations: government share to 2 decimals, jobs per employed resident to 3 decimals, and the industry concentration index to a whole number.

values.0: All ownerships (total covered). Used for jobs, establishments, wages and average pay.
values.5: Private ownership, which includes nonprofit organizations. Used for private jobs and for every industry variable.
values.1: Federal government. The observatory downloads these rows but does not publish them in its data file.
values.2: State government (the Commonwealth in Puerto Rico). The observatory downloads these rows but does not publish them in its data file.
values.3: Local government (municipal). The observatory downloads these rows but does not publish them in its data file.
values.disclosure code N: BLS withholds the figures of the row to protect an employer's confidentiality. The observatory leaves the cell blank.

source_detail: BLS QCEW open-data API, annual-average area files: https://data.bls.gov/cew/data/api/<year>/a/area/<area>.csv, where <area> is the five-digit FIPS (Federal Information Processing Standards) code of the municipio (72001 Adjuntas, 72003 Aguada, and so on up to 72153 Yauco; 78 codes in all) or 72000 for Puerto Rico. Columns used: own_code, industry_code, disclosure_code, annual_avg_estabs, annual_avg_emplvl, total_annual_wages, avg_annual_pay. File layout: https://www.bls.gov/cew/additional-resources/open-data/ . Who is covered: https://www.bls.gov/cew/overview.htm . NAICS editions by year: https://www.bls.gov/cew/classifications/industry/home.htm .
how_to_read: Read every QCEW figure as what employers located in the municipality reported, not as what the residents do. A blank is not a zero: it means BLS withheld the figure or publishes no row for that cell. Use the Puerto Rico value as BLS's island figure; it is not the sum of the 78 municipalities. Treat the latest year (2025 in the 2026-10 snapshot) as preliminary. On the Analysis tab, a jobs count can be shown as published, per 1,000 residents, per square kilometer, as a share of the island total, as a share of the municipality's jobs, or as a location quotient. A location quotient is the industry's share of the municipality's jobs divided by its share of the island's jobs; above 1 means the industry is more concentrated here than on the island, and below 1 means less. The share and the quotient use total jobs (all employers, including government) of the same year as the divisor. The observatory downloaded every year's file on 3 October 2026. It keeps each file and reads it again only on a full refresh, so a later BLS revision, including to preliminary 2025, shows only after a refresh. The 'Data built' date in the dataset information window is the day the observatory's data file was last rebuilt, which can be later than the download. When you cite a figure, give the year, the ownership and industry row, and the retrieval date. The examples in these entries come from the 2026-10 snapshot. They use 2025 for totals (jobs, wages, pay), which have a value for every municipality, and 2024 for industry sectors, because 2025 has fewer published municipal values for sectors.
caveats: Coverage. BLS says covered employment is about 95% of jobs in the United States. The observatory does not measure the share for Puerto Rico. Not counted: proprietors and other self-employed people, unpaid family workers, informal or off-the-books work, military and National Guard members, elected officials, railroad workers covered by their own system, certain farm and domestic workers, and anyone who did not work or get paid in the pay period that includes the 12th of the month. BLS lists a few further small groups at https://www.bls.gov/cew/overview.htm .

Jobs, not people. A person with two jobs at two employers counts twice. A job at a company with several sites is counted at the site that the employer reports; if an employer reports all its workers under one site, they appear in that site's municipality. The observatory cannot test how each employer reports.

Two kinds of blank. In the BLS files, a blank industry cell is either withheld (disclosure code N) or has no row. BLS's file layout notes do not say why a row is absent, so the observatory cannot tell from the files whether a missing row means that the place has no employer in that industry. The published data file does not tell the two kinds apart. In the 2026-10 snapshot, across the 19 sectors and the 78 municipalities in 2024, 769 cells have a value, 527 are withheld and 186 have no row (of 1,482).

Blanks are most common in small municipalities and in narrow industries. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the 26 municipalities with the fewest jobs in 2024 have a value in 6.5 of the 19 sectors on average; the 26 with the most jobs have 13.0. Some hidden cells look paired: in the same snapshot, 19 municipalities have the sector 72 total (hotels and restaurants) published in 2024 while both of its parts, accommodation (721) and food service (722), are blank.

The Puerto Rico value is BLS's own island figure. In the 2026-10 snapshot, it is above the sum of the 78 municipalities by 1,681 jobs (0.2%) in 2014 and by 4,555 (0.5%) in 2025. BLS's files do not give the reason. In the same snapshot, for industries the island cell is blank while municipal cells are published (construction in 2025), and it is published while almost every municipal cell is blank (mining in 2024).

In the 2026-10 snapshot, 2025 is the latest year and is preliminary: BLS can revise it. It is also less complete: 13 of the 19 sectors have fewer municipalities with a published value in 2025 than in 2024, and five sectors (mining, utilities, construction, transportation and warehousing, information) have no island value in 2025.
Annual averages smooth changes inside a year. An event in September (such as Hurricane Maria in 2017) shows part of its effect in that year and part in the next.

The sector definitions follow NAICS, which is revised every five years. BLS classified 2014 to 2016 data with NAICS 2012, 2017 to 2021 data with NAICS 2017 and 2022 onward with NAICS 2022 (see the BLS industry classification page). The observatory does not recode earlier years to one edition, so a sector total before and after 2017 or 2022 may not be fully comparable. Check the BLS notes before reading a small change at sector level as real.

BLS also reports government jobs by level (federal, state, local, ownership codes 1, 2 and 3). The observatory downloads them but publishes only the total minus private, so government jobs cannot be split by level in this data.

name: Jobs per employed resident
plain: How many jobs are located in the municipality for each employed resident. Above 1 means more jobs than employed residents live there, so the place may draw workers from elsewhere. Below 1 means fewer jobs than employed residents. Many of those residents may work elsewhere, or in work that the jobs data do not count, such as self-employment.
definition: Jobs located in the municipality (annual average, from the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) of the US Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS)) divided by employed residents 16 and over (civilian, from the American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates) whose survey window ends in the same year. For 2024 the residents are those of the 2020 to 2024 window. The jobs figure is one year; the residents figure is a five-year window.

coverage.frequency: One value per year when both inputs exist. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 2025 is missing because the ACS window ending in 2025 is not published yet.

method: Calculated by the observatory: round(qcew_jobs / workers_16plus, 3) for each year and place where both are above zero. workers_16plus is the ACS count of civilian employed residents 16 and over (table B24080, total), described in the entry for employed residents. The island value divides BLS's island jobs by the ACS island count of employed residents, which equals the sum of the 78 municipalities' counts.
source_detail: Jobs: BLS QCEW, ownership 0, industry 10, annual_avg_emplvl. Residents: ACS 5-year estimates, table B24080, total, window ending in the same year (summary files at https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/summary_file/).
how_to_read: A value of 1 means one covered job for each employed resident. Compare a municipality with the island value, not with 1. A value well above the island value points to a place that draws workers; a low value points to a place where many residents work elsewhere. It does not say where they work. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island value is 0.82 in 2024, below 1; one reason is that the jobs count leaves out self-employed and informal work, which the resident count includes. That year, 9 of 78 municipalities are above 1: San Juan (1.91), Mayagüez (1.52), Guaynabo (1.50), Cataño (1.44), Barceloneta (1.27), Aguadilla (1.21), Ponce (1.20), Manatí (1.19), Humacao (1.05). The middle municipal value is 0.50, so a typical municipality has about one covered job for every two employed residents. The lowest is Toa Alta (0.16), and Toa Alta is the lowest in every year from 2014 to 2024.
caveats: It compares two different counts. It is consistent with commuting but does not measure it. For commuting itself, see the commute variables from the same survey.
The years do not match exactly. A QCEW year is divided by a five-year survey window that ends in that year, so the 2020 jobs dip is divided by a window that covers 2016 to 2020.

The resident count is a survey estimate with a margin of error (90% confidence). In the 2026-10 snapshot, the 2024 margin is about 6% of the estimate in a typical municipality and 19% in Culebra. The margin is not carried into the ratio.
The jobs are counted at the employer's reporting site, so a company that reports all its workers under one site raises the ratio there.
Jobs are not people: a person with two jobs counts twice in the numerator and once in the denominator.
A low value can also reflect self-employed or informal workers, who are in the resident count but not in the jobs count.
In the 2026-10 snapshot, all 78 municipalities have a value in each year from 2014 to 2024, and the island count of employed residents is 1,150,831 in 2024.

name: Industry concentration (Herfindahl index)
plain: A score of how concentrated the local jobs are in a few industries. A low score means jobs are spread across many industries; a high score means a few, often government, hold most of them.
definition: The Herfindahl-Hirschman index (HHI) of the job shares of the municipality's industries. Each industry's share of all local jobs is squared and the squares are added and multiplied by 10,000. The industries are the 19 private sectors of the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) that the US Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) publishes for the municipality, plus government as one group. It is calculated only where the published sectors and government cover at least 80% of all jobs. It is also blank where private jobs are withheld, because government jobs cannot then be worked out.

coverage.frequency: One value per calendar year. When the observatory's data are rebuilt, it checks whether BLS has published a newer year. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 2025 is the latest year and is preliminary.

method: Calculated by the observatory. For each municipality and year: total jobs T = qcew_jobs. Government G = total jobs minus private jobs. Each published private sector gives S, its jobs. The sectors and government are 'covered' if (sum of S + G) / T is at least 0.8. If so, HHI = round(10,000 x sum of (jobs / T)^2) over the published sectors and government; the shares are of all jobs, including government, and a hidden sector adds nothing. If not, the value is blank. It can be recomputed from the published sector values. The value is also blank where private jobs are withheld, because government jobs cannot then be worked out. The Analysis tab's inspector also names the largest employer group (see its entry). That group uses the same sector values but has no 80% test.
source_detail: BLS QCEW open-data API, annual-average area files: https://data.bls.gov/cew/data/api/<year>/a/area/<area>.csv, where <area> is the five-digit FIPS (Federal Information Processing Standards) code of the municipio (72001 Adjuntas, 72003 Aguada, and so on up to 72153 Yauco; 78 codes in all) or 72000 for Puerto Rico. Rows: own_code 5 for the 19 sectors, plus own_code 0 and own_code 5 with industry_code 10 for total and government jobs.
how_to_read: Lower is more diversified. With jobs spread evenly over the 20 groups the score is 500; with all jobs in one group it is 10,000. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the 2024 municipal values run from 814 (Guaynabo) to 5,940 (Maunabo), and the island value is 1,040 (built from all 19 sectors). A high value can come from one large private sector or from a large government share, because government counts as one group. The score compares places and years within this data. It is not a measure of economic health. The inspector's 'largest employer group' ignores hidden sectors and counts government as one group, so it can name Government or a smaller sector when a larger sector is withheld; see its entry.
caveats: Government is treated as one group. A municipality where government holds most jobs scores high mainly for that reason. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Maunabo has the highest value in 2024, with a government share of 76%.

Jobs in hidden sectors are left out, so a score can be too low but not too high, compared with a calculation that had every sector. Up to 20% of jobs can be missing from the calculation, because of the 80% rule.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, many municipalities have no value: 19 in 2014, 30 in 2024 and 38 in 2025. A municipality can enter or leave the set from one year to the next as BLS hides or shows sectors, so do not read a change that comes with a change in the set of published sectors as a trend.
It uses only 20 groups, and the private sectors are broad. It does not see concentration inside a sector, such as one large employer.
In the 2026-10 snapshot, 2025 is the latest year and is preliminary: BLS can revise it.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island value uses all 19 sectors except in 2015 (sector 81 missing), 2022 (sector 51 missing) and 2025 (five sectors missing: mining, utilities, construction, transportation and warehousing, information). In 2025 the published sectors and government cover 91.8% of jobs, and with those five sectors held at their 2024 size the score would be about 1,026, not 1,004. In 2015 and 2022 the gap is about 3 points. 2024 is the latest island value built from all 19 sectors, so do not read the 2024 to 2025 island change as a trend.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, among the 48 municipalities with a value in 2024, smaller ones tend to score higher: the rank correlation with total jobs is about -0.63 (-1 would mean the order is exactly reversed). The 30 municipalities without a value tend to be small (median 3,036 jobs, against 7,084 for those with a value). A high score is not by itself a sign of a weak economy.

Do not compare a municipality's score with the island's. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island figure has almost every sector published in every year; a municipality often does not, and a score built from fewer sectors is lower.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island value exists in every year. Culebra's value is blank in 2015 to 2021 because its private jobs are withheld, and in 2022 to 2025 because the published sectors and government cover less than 80% of its jobs.

coverage.frequency: One value per calendar year, rebuilt with the jobs data. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 2025 is the latest year and is preliminary.

method: Calculated by the observatory together with the industry concentration index. It includes hotels, resorts, inns and guesthouses, and restaurants, fast-food outlets, cafes, bars, food trucks and caterers. It is the sum of accommodation (721) and food service (722), to within one job from rounding. The data come from the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) of the US Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS). Only wage-and-salary jobs are counted, each at the work site. A blank means that BLS withholds the figure to protect an employer's confidentiality, or publishes no row for the sector there. It does not mean zero.

coverage.frequency: One value per calendar year. When the observatory's data are rebuilt, it checks whether BLS has published a newer year. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 2025 is the latest year and is preliminary.

method: Column annual_avg_emplvl of the BLS annual file for each municipality and year, ownership code 5 (private), industry code 72. A row that BLS marks as withheld (disclosure code N) is left blank. A municipality with no row for the sector is also blank (BLS's file layout does not say why a row is absent). The Puerto Rico value is BLS's own island figure, not a sum of the municipalities.
source_detail: BLS QCEW open-data API, annual-average area files: https://data.bls.gov/cew/data/api/<year>/a/area/<area>.csv, where <area> is the five-digit FIPS (Federal Information Processing Standards) code of the municipio (72001 Adjuntas, 72003 Aguada, and so on up to 72153 Yauco; 78 codes in all) or 72000 for Puerto Rico. how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island total is 76,407 in 2014 and 90,930 in 2024 (19.0% higher), and 93,288 in 2025. It is 12.1% of island private jobs in 2024. The largest published municipal values in 2024 are San Juan (23,751), Carolina (6,896), Bayamón (5,292). The published municipal values add up to 85% of the island figure in 2024, so 15% of the island figure is not in them (hidden cells, plus a gap that BLS's files do not explain: BLS's island private jobs are 0.5% above the sum of the 78 municipalities in 2024). On the Analysis tab you can also shade it as a share of local jobs or as a location quotient (see the QCEW method entry).
caveats: A map of this variable mostly shows where BLS publishes the figure, not only where the jobs are. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 44 of the 78 municipalities have a value in 2024.

The parts, accommodation (721) and food service (722), are often both blank even when this total is published, so the total cannot be split. In the 2026-10 snapshot, this is so for 19 municipalities in 2024.

plain: Private jobs in repair shops, hair and nail salons, funeral homes, churches and civic groups in the municipality.
definition: Annual-average jobs at private employers located in the municipality, in sector 81 of the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS), other services (except public administration).
